title: The Creek Is the Curriculum: How Bloom's Taxonomy Actually Works
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Stinehart argues that Bloom's Taxonomy is misused as a linear checklist of higher-order questions when it actually describes how minds move, and that it is most visible in unstructured play. He walks through each tier of the taxonomy and shows children remembering, analysing, evaluating and creating during imaginative play. A three-hour creek dam built by his daughter and a friend, and examples from his school's Play Club, serve as evidence. He redefines rigor as depth, sustained thinking and revision without shame rather than difficulty. The piece cites bodies such as the AAP and OECD in support of play, and ends by urging teachers to watch rather than interrogate. It is largely anecdotal and sits against explicit-instruction approaches, but it states a clear claim about learning and curriculum.
points: Bloom's tiers are not a ladder climbed in order; children move through all six levels at once during play.
The creek dam anecdote illustrates hypothesis, testing, iteration and systems thinking arising without any learning objective.
Rigor is redefined as depth, sustained thinking and risk without guarantees, not difficulty or rubric compliance.
Constantly asking children what they are learning turns learning into performance, so teachers should observe instead.
quotes: We say we’re scaffolding students up the pyramid, but too often we’re just checking boxes, “ask a higher-order question,” “differentiate by tier.” We treat the taxonomy like a to-do list. But Bloom was never a list guy.
Play isn’t what happens after learning. It’s what learning looks like in motion. Every tier of Bloom’s? It’s already baked into play.
They scavenged materials: broken PVC, rocks, sticks, even two discarded cinder blocks. They built, failed, rebuilt. They tested flow, redirected water, debated, redesigned.
If you want to see Bloom’s Taxonomy in action, don’t look at a lesson plan. Look at a muddy hand adjusting a broken PVC pipe.
Another week, a group of girls turned a pile of cardboard into a restaurant. Handwritten menus. Price tiers. One girl acted as manager.
We have a national fear of downtime. If we give kids too much space, we think they’ll fall behind. We treat unstructured play like a luxury.
We love asking kids, “What are you learning?” It sounds good. But it yanks them out of the moment. It turns learning into performance.
